extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of legal doctrines governing what a patent may lawfully claim (unity of invention, inventorship, foreign applicant rights, extensions, assignments). Explains limits on combining inventions, requirements for the specification, and who may obtain or extend patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and distinctness of specification and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The validity of a patent materially depends upon the accuracy and distinctness with which the invention is stated in the specification; when a patentee states and sums up the particulars of his invention in his specification and his patent covers them, he is confined to such summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts cannot reject a claim that the patentee asserts as his own in the specification; but if something included in the patent is not new, the patent may be void. The patentee cannot afterwards broaden beyond what is summed up in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of claimed subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If any part which the patentee claims in his specification as his invention is not new (even if of slight value), and is included in the patent, the patent may be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that covers matter already in public use or known is fatal. The inventor's honest mistake about being first does not save the claim. (Act of 1837 provides a limited mitigation—see separate entry.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the subject-matter (single invention principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent under the general patent acts cannot embrace various distinct improvements and inventions for unconnected objects; the statute contemplates a definite and single invention as the 'thing patented.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct and independent inventions having no common connection or purpose should be the subject of separate patents; joining them in one patent is inconsistent with statutory language and common law doctrine and may render the patent void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible combination: several improvements in one machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Several distinct improvements in one machine may be united in one patent as improvements of the same machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to include multiple improvements to a single machine in one patent because they relate to a single subject-matter; this contrasts with attempting to include improvements in different machines having no common purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible combination: distinct machines if auxiliary to same end
rubrics_metrics.description: Where different machines invented by the patentee conduce to the same common purpose and object, though capable of distinct use, they may be united in one patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If distinct machines are auxiliary to the same general end (several modes to accomplish a single object), unity of the subject-matter is preserved and they may lawfully be joined; the subject-matter then consists of the object to be accomplished and the several modes of accomplishing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impermissible combination: totally distinct machines for different objects
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent cannot be taken for two distinct machines not conducing to the same common purpose or object, but designed for totally distinct and independent objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventions are wholly independent and for unconnected objects, they should be patented separately; otherwise difficulties arise (e.g., if one is not new, whether entire patent is void).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must fully explain principle and several modes
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent statute requires that the inventor 'fully explain the principle and the several modes, in which he has contemplated the application of that principle,' by which the invention may be distinguished from others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory duty supports including in one patent all the modes and modifications contemplated by the inventor for applying the same principle, provided they are new and relate to the same general end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct claim of inventorship (sole vs joint inventors)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be claimed as the sole invention of one party if that is the fact, or as the joint invention of two or more parties if it was invented by more than one; a party who claims a joint invention as sole (or vice versa) encounters invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joint invention may be patented jointly; a sole inventor cannot take a joint patent for what was solely his, and a joint inventor cannot take a sole patent. The statute contemplates joint inventions and requires appropriate oath/affirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No two subsisting patents for the same invention; estoppel of prior grant
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor cannot have two subsisting valid patents at the same time for the same invention; the first patent, while in force, is an estoppel to any subsequent patent by the same person for the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subsequent patent inconsistent with prior grant is estopped; similarly, obtaining sole and joint patents for the same subject raises inconsistency and may void one or the other. The rule prevents prolonging exclusivity by successive grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alien inventor eligibility and foreign-patent/public-use limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien who is the original and first inventor of a patentable subject may apply for and obtain a U.S. patent in the same manner as a citizen; statutes address prior foreign patents and publication within six months and prior introduction into public use in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the Acts of 1836 and 1839: if an alien patented or published abroad, he may still obtain a U.S. patent provided the subject was not introduced into public and common use in the U.S. before application; the six-month window from foreign patent/publication is significant and the patent office treats foreign enrolment/enrolment date as controlling in interference situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of patents: who may apply and evidentiary requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The 18th section (Act of 1836) allows extension of a patent beyond its term upon application by the patentee (inventor), with prescribed notice and evidence; the patentee must furnish under oath a statement of the ascertained value of the invention and his receipts and expenditures to exhibit a true account of loss and profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The board (secretary of state, commissioner, solicitor of treasury) must be 'fully and entirely satisfied' that extension is just and proper, having due regard to public interest, and that the inventor (not assignee) without neglect or fault failed to attain reasonable remuneration. No extension is to be granted after expiration of the original term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit of extensions to assignees and licensees is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: The benefit of a renewed patent shall extend to assignees and grantees of the right to use the thing patented to the extent of their respective interest therein, but does not enlarge their rights beyond the interest originally granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignees under the original patent do not automatically acquire rights under the extended patent unless expressly conveyed or necessarily implied by the original assignment; assignees in use at time of renewal may continue to use but do not gain making/selling rights unless conveyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments and licenses cannot convey future or non-existent rights at law
rubrics_metrics.description: A grant or assignment can only pass rights actually possessed at the time; an assignment of a right not yet in existence (e.g., future renewal rights) is, at law, ineffective except as a covenant/enforceable contract in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensees/assignees whose grants were limited to the original term do not automatically share in renewals; equity may enforce covenants made to secure future benefits when the right comes into existence, but at law the assignment is limited to present rights.
